title: Cells and their organisation I – cell theory, prokaryotes vs eukaryotes, organelles, membranes and transport
blurb: History and principles of cell theory; the origin of cells (Earth 4.6 billion years, first organic molecules 4.0–4.2, first cells 3.8; LUCA → bacteria and archaea).
h1: Cells and their organisation I – cell theory, prokaryotes vs eukaryotes, organelles, membranes and transport
lede: History and principles of cell theory; the origin of cells (Earth 4.6 billion years, first organic molecules 4.0–4.2, first cells 3.8; LUCA → bacteria and archaea). A detailed prokaryote vs eukaryote comparison, prokaryotic structure (surface layers, flagella, nucleoid, plasmids) and eukaryotic organelles: nucleus, chromatin, ribosomes (70S vs 80S), ER, Golgi, vesicles, mitochondria, plastids and the cytoskeleton (3 filament types). Then plant vs animal cells, biological membranes (phospholipids, glycolipids, cholesterol; asymmetry; membrane proteins) and membrane transport: passive (simple and facilitated diffusion, channels) vs active (transporters, symport, ATP pumps, the Na⁺/K⁺ pump).

items.n: Who first used the word "cell", and when?
items.a: Robert Hooke, 1665, looking at cork.

items.n: Who said cells arise only from other living cells?
items.a: Rudolf Virchow (~1850).

items.n: Who proposed in 1839 that cells are the basic unit of life?
items.a: Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann.
All organisms are made of cells; cells are the basic units of life; all cells come from existing cells.

items.n: When did the first cells appear?
items.a: About 3.8 billion years ago (Earth formed 4.6 billion).

items.n: Which two groups arose from LUCA?
items.a: Bacteria and archaea.
Pro- (before) + karyon (kernel): an organism without a nucleus.
By binary fission.
Cell membrane (semipermeable), cell wall (peptidoglycan), capsule (polysaccharides).
Movement of bacteria along a chemical gradient (e.g. toward glucose) using flagella.

items.n: What are plasmids, and why are they important?
items.a: Extra-chromosomal circular DNA; their exchange spreads antibiotic resistance.

items.n: Of what is the eukaryotic cell wall made?
items.a: Cellulose (plants, algae) or chitin (fungi, insects, crustaceans); never murein.
rRNA synthesis.
Fibrous proteins of the inner nuclear membrane (structure, gene regulation); mutations cause laminopathies.
Prokaryotic 70S (30S + 50S); eukaryotic 80S (40S + 60S).
Rough: protein synthesis, folding, glycosylation. Smooth: lipids, hormones, calcium metabolism.
Completes modification of ER products and sends them in vesicles to their destination.
Hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion.
Protect the cell from hydrogen peroxide using specific enzymes.

items.n: Which processes take place in mitochondria?
items.a: Citrate cycle, β-oxidation of fatty acids (and ATP production).
An archaeal cell engulfed an aerobic bacterium (endosymbiosis).
They have their own circular DNA and protein-synthesis apparatus.
Leukoplasts (storage), chromoplasts (carotenes, xanthophylls), chloroplasts (chlorophyll).
Stacks of thylakoids in chloroplasts.

items.n: Thickest cytoskeletal fibre and its protein?
items.a: Microtubules, 25 nm, tubulin.

items.n: Thinnest cytoskeletal fibre and its protein?
items.a: Microfilaments, 5–9 nm, actin.

items.n: Diameter and role of intermediate filaments?
items.a: 8–12 nm; strength, anchoring the nucleus and desmosomes, nuclear lamina.

items.n: Which filaments form the mitotic spindle, cilia and flagella?
items.a: Microtubules.

items.n: Which organelles do plants have but animals lack?
items.a: Cell wall, plastids, a large central vacuole, glyoxysomes.

items.n: How thick is the lipid bilayer?
items.a: About 5 nm.
Phospholipids, glycolipids, cholesterol.
Different lipids on each side, e.g. glycolipids only on the non-cytosolic side.

items.n: What share of animal proteins are membrane proteins?
items.a: About 30 %.
Transporters bind, change shape and release; channels are continuous selective pores with weak binding.

items.n: Three energy sources for active transport?
items.a: A concentration/electrochemical gradient, ATP hydrolysis, light.

items.n: What does the Na⁺/K⁺ pump do?
items.a: Per ATP, pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in (P-type pump).

items.n: Which pump makes most of the cell's ATP?
items.a: F-type ATPase (in mitochondria).

items.n: How does glucose enter intestinal cells?
items.a: Na⁺–glucose symport, driven by the Na⁺ gradient kept by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.
